title: Programming and Data Structures
description: Master C programming fundamentals, memory layout, arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs for the IOCL and GATE CS exams.

topics.title: C Language Fundamentals
topics.whyItMatters: C language syntax, operator precedence, and memory layout form the foundation of many execution-trace MCQs.
understandSimply: Think of C programming as building blocks: variables are boxes holding data, operators are the tools to modify them, and pointers are just maps showing where the boxes live in memory.
technicalExplanation: C is a statically typed, compiled language. Execution begins at `main()`. Memory is divided into Text (code), Data (initialized globals), BSS (uninitialized globals), Heap (dynamic allocation), and Stack (local variables and function calls). Operator precedence dictates evaluation order (e.g., postfix `++` has higher precedence than prefix `++` or dereference `*`). Pointers store memory addresses of other variables.

definitions.definition: A variable that stores the memory address of another variable.
In C, an array name decays to a constant pointer to its first element.

steps.title: Evaluate Precedence
steps.description: Identify the operators with the highest precedence in the expression.

steps.title: Check Associativity
steps.description: For operators with the same precedence, evaluate based on their associativity (usually Left-to-Right, but Right-to-Left for assignment and unary operators).

steps.title: Compute Value
steps.description: Resolve the expression step-by-step, updating variable states carefully, especially for post/pre-increment.

solvedExamples.solution: If forced to evaluate L-to-R: `x++` evaluates to 5 (x becomes 6). `++x` evaluates to 7 (x becomes 7). Sum = 12. Note: Modifying a variable twice between sequence points is Undefined Behavior in standard C, but exams sometimes assume a strict evaluation order.
solvedExamples.question: What is the output of: `int x = 5; printf("%d", x++ + ++x);`? (Assume undefined behavior is evaluated left-to-right strictly for academic purposes, though technically undefined).

solvedExamples.solution: `p` points to `arr[0]`. `p+1` points to `arr[1]` because pointer arithmetic scales by `sizeof(int)`. Dereferencing it yields 2.
solvedExamples.question: If `int arr[] = {1, 2, 3}; int *p = arr;`, what does `*(p+1)` evaluate to?

traps: Confusing post-increment `x++` (use then increment) with pre-increment `++x` (increment then use).
Assuming `sizeof(pointer)` equals the size of the array it points to (it's the size of the memory address, usually 4 or 8 bytes).
takeaways: Array names decay into pointers when passed to functions.
Pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the data type.
Global variables are initialized to zero by default; local variables contain garbage.
Prefix operators and assignment evaluate Right-to-Left.
Modifying a variable multiple times in an expression without sequence points leads to Undefined Behavior.

quickRecall.question: Does an array name passed to a function pass by value or reference?
quickRecall.answer: It passes the memory address (decayed pointer), effectively passing by reference.

quickRecall.question: What is the default value of an uninitialized global variable in C?
What does `*p++` do?
quickRecall.answer: Dereferences `p`, then increments the pointer `p` (due to postfix `++` precedence over unary `*`).

topics.title: Functions and Recursion
topics.whyItMatters: Recursive function tracing is guaranteed to appear in exams, testing your ability to manually manage the call stack.
understandSimply: Recursion is like looking into a mirror reflecting another mirror. You keep diving deeper until you hit a wall (the base case), and then you climb back out, combining the results.
technicalExplanation: Functions use Activation Records (stack frames) to store local variables, parameters, and return addresses. Recursion occurs when a function calls itself. Every recursive call pushes a new frame onto the call stack. The base case prevents infinite recursion. Variables declared `static` within a function retain their value across multiple calls and are stored in the Data segment, not the Stack.

definitions.definition: The condition under which a recursive function returns without making further calls.
A recursive function where the recursive call is the absolute last operation performed.

steps.title: Identify the Base Case
steps.description: Find the condition that stops the recursion.

steps.title: Draw a Recursion Tree
steps.description: Sketch the function calls, passing the updated parameters to each child node.

steps.title: Trace the Returns
steps.description: Propagate the returned values back up the tree to the root.

comparison.title: Iteration vs Recursion
comparison.description: Iteration uses loops and has lower memory overhead. Recursion uses function calls (stack memory) and is often cleaner for hierarchical data like trees, but risks Stack Overflow.

solvedExamples.solution: `f(3)` calls `3 * f(2)`. `f(2)` calls `2 * f(1)`. `f(1)` returns 1. Resolving: `f(2)` returns 2. `f(3)` returns 6.
solvedExamples.question: Trace `int f(int n) { if(n<=1) return 1; return n * f(n-1); }` for `f(3)`.

solvedExamples.solution: The `count` variable is initialized only once. Every recursive call increments the exact same memory location, tracking the total number of calls across all frames.
solvedExamples.question: What happens if a recursive function has a `static int count = 0; count++;`?

traps: Forgetting that local variables are unique to each recursive call.
Missing print statements that occur *after* the recursive call (evaluated during the return phase).
Assuming `static` variables are reset on each recursive call.
takeaways: Every recursive call creates a new stack frame.
Tail recursion can be optimized by compilers into a simple loop to save stack space.
Tree recursion (multiple recursive calls in one function) causes exponential time complexity without memoization.
Static variables persist across all function calls.
Tracing recursion requires careful attention to pre-call and post-call operations.

quickRecall.question: Where are local variables of a recursive function stored?
What is tail recursion?
quickRecall.answer: When the recursive call is the final statement executed in the function.

quickRecall.question: Do static variables get re-initialized on every recursive call?
quickRecall.answer: No, they are initialized only once.

topics.title: Structures and Dynamic Memory
topics.whyItMatters: Understanding heap allocation and structure padding is essential for analyzing memory efficiency and detecting memory leaks.
understandSimply: Structures let you group different data types into one package. Dynamic memory is like renting storage space while the program runs; you must remember to return it when you're done, or you'll run out of space.
technicalExplanation: A `struct` allocates contiguous memory for all its members, often inserting padding bytes to satisfy hardware alignment requirements. A `union` allocates memory equal to its largest member, and all members share that same memory location. Dynamic memory is requested from the Heap using `malloc()` (uninitialized) or `calloc()` (zero-initialized), and released using `free()`. Failing to `free()` causes memory leaks; using a pointer after `free()` causes a dangling pointer.

definitions.definition: Extra bytes added between struct members to align data in memory for faster CPU access.
Occurs when dynamically allocated memory is not freed before the last pointer to it is lost.
A pointer that references a memory location that has already been freed.

steps.title: Calculate Struct Size
steps.description: Identify the largest primitive member type to determine the alignment boundary.

steps.title: Align Members
steps.description: Place each member in memory, adding padding bytes so its address is a multiple of its size.

steps.title: Pad the End
steps.description: Add padding at the end of the struct so the total size is a multiple of the largest alignment boundary.

solvedExamples.solution: `c` takes 1 byte. 3 bytes padding are added to align `i` (4 bytes). `i` takes 4 bytes. `d` takes 1 byte. 3 bytes padding are added at the end so the total size is a multiple of 4. Total = $1 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 12$ bytes.
solvedExamples.question: Size of `struct { char c; int i; char d; }` on a 32-bit system?

solvedExamples.solution: `malloc` allocates a block of 40 bytes containing garbage values. `calloc` allocates 40 bytes and initializes all bits to zero.
solvedExamples.question: Difference between `malloc(10 * sizeof(int))` and `calloc(10, sizeof(int))`?

traps: Assuming the size of a struct is exactly the sum of its members' sizes.
Using `sizeof` on a dynamically allocated array pointer (returns pointer size, not array size).
Returning a pointer to a local variable from a function.
takeaways: Structs use padding for alignment; Unions share memory space.
Dynamic memory (Heap) must be manually managed using `malloc`/`calloc` and `free`.
Memory leaks happen when references to heap memory are lost without calling `free`.
Dangling pointers occur when memory is freed but the pointer is still used.
Pointer arithmetic on struct pointers jumps by the padded size of the struct.

quickRecall.question: What is the size of a union?
quickRecall.answer: The size of its largest member.

quickRecall.question: What does `calloc` do that `malloc` does not?
quickRecall.answer: It initializes the allocated memory to zero.

quickRecall.question: What is a dangling pointer?
quickRecall.answer: A pointer pointing to a freed memory location.

topics.title: Linear Data Structures (Arrays & Linked Lists)
topics.whyItMatters: Arrays and Linked Lists are the building blocks for all other data structures. 2D array mapping formulas are common numerical questions.
understandSimply: Arrays are like a row of connected houses with numbered addresses—you can instantly jump to any house. Linked lists are like a treasure hunt—each clue only points to the next location.
technicalExplanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, allowing $O(1)$ random access but $O(N)$ insertions/deletions. 2D arrays are mapped to 1D memory using Row-Major or Column-Major order. Linked Lists consist of nodes (data + pointer). They allow $O(1)$ insertions/deletions if the location is known, but require $O(N)$ traversal to find elements. Doubly Linked Lists have pointers to both next and previous nodes; Circular Linked Lists point the last node back to the first.

definitions.definition: Storing a 2D array row by row in contiguous memory.
Storing a 2D array column by column in contiguous memory.

steps.title: Insert at Head of Linked List
steps.description: Create new node. Set its next to current head. Update head pointer to new node.

steps.title: Delete a Node
steps.description: Find the node and its predecessor. Set predecessor's next to the target node's next. Free the target node.

formula.expression: Loc(A[i][j]) = Base + [(i - LB1) * N + (j - LB2)] * w
formula.explanation: Row-major order address. N is number of columns, w is element size in bytes. LB1/LB2 are lower bounds of row/col indices.
formula.whenToUse: To find the memory address of an element in a 2D array stored in row-major order.

formula.expression: Loc(A[i][j]) = Base + [(j - LB2) * M + (i - LB1)] * w
formula.explanation: Column-major order address. M is number of rows.
formula.whenToUse: To find the memory address of an element in a 2D array stored in column-major order.

solvedExamples.question: Given `A[10][20]` with base address 100, element size 2 bytes, 0-indexed. Find address of `A[5][10]` in Row-Major order.

solvedExamples.solution: Use three pointers: `prev` (NULL), `curr` (head), `next`. In a loop: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next;`. Update head to `prev`.
solvedExamples.question: Reverse a singly linked list in $O(N)$ time.

traps: Confusing Row-Major (multiply by columns $N$) with Column-Major (multiply by rows $M$).
Losing the rest of the linked list during insertion by updating the previous node's pointer before storing the next node's address.
Assuming array indices always start at 0 (exams may give arrays like $A[1..10]$).
takeaways: Arrays have $O(1)$ access, $O(N)$ insertion/deletion.
Linked lists have $O(N)$ access, $O(1)$ insertion/deletion (if pointer is known).
Row-major order multiplies row offset by the number of columns.
Column-major order multiplies column offset by the number of rows.
Always update the `next` pointer of a new node before breaking the existing links.

quickRecall.question: What is the time complexity to access the $k$-th element in a Linked List?
In a 2D array `A[M][N]`, which dimension multiplier is used in Row-Major order?
What happens if you update `head = new_node` before `new_node->next = head`?
quickRecall.answer: You lose the reference to the original list (memory leak).

topics.title: Stacks
topics.whyItMatters: Stacks are fundamental for parsing, expression evaluation, and recursion. Postfix evaluation is a guaranteed MCQ type.
understandSimply: A stack is like a stack of plates. You can only put a new plate on the top (Push), and you can only take the top plate off (Pop). Last-In, First-Out (LIFO).
technicalExplanation: A Stack is a LIFO data structure. Operations `push()` and `pop()` run in $O(1)$ time. Stacks can be implemented using arrays (fixed size, requires bounds checking) or linked lists (dynamic size, insert/delete at head). They are heavily used in compilers for syntax parsing, recursion, and converting Infix expressions to Postfix/Prefix.

definitions.definition: Last-In, First-Out. The last element added is the first one removed.
Operators are written after their operands (e.g., `A B +`). Also known as Reverse Polish Notation.

steps.title: Evaluate Postfix Expression
steps.description: Scan from left to right.

steps.title: Process Operands
steps.description: If the token is an operand (number), Push it onto the stack.

steps.title: Process Operators
steps.description: If the token is an operator, Pop two operands ($A$ then $B$), evaluate $B 	ext{ op } A$, and Push the result back.

solvedExamples.solution: Push 5, Push 3. Read `+`: Pop 3, Pop 5, evaluate $5+3=8$, Push 8. Read `2`: Push 2. Read `*`: Pop 2, Pop 8, evaluate $8*2=16$, Push 16. Result is 16.
solvedExamples.question: Evaluate the postfix expression: `5 3 + 2 *`

solvedExamples.solution: `*` has higher precedence than `+`. `B * C` becomes `B C *`. Then add `A`: `A B C * +`.
solvedExamples.question: Convert infix `A + B * C` to postfix.

traps: In postfix evaluation, evaluating $A 	ext{ op } B$ instead of $B 	ext{ op } A$ when popping (matters for subtraction and division).
Assuming stack depth equals string length (depth depends on the sequence of operators and operands).
takeaways: Stacks follow LIFO (Last-In, First-Out).
Push and Pop operations are $O(1)$.
When evaluating postfix, the first popped element is the right operand, the second popped is the left operand.
Infix to Postfix conversion uses a stack for operators based on precedence and associativity.
Parentheses matching is a classic stack application.

quickRecall.question: What is the time complexity of Push and Pop?
In postfix `A B /`, what is the division operation?
quickRecall.answer: $A / B$ (second popped element divided by first popped element).

quickRecall.question: What principle does a stack follow?

topics.title: Queues
topics.whyItMatters: Queues are used in OS scheduling and Graph BFS. Circular queue boundary conditions are heavily tested.
understandSimply: A queue is like a line at a ticket counter. The first person to join the line is the first person served. First-In, First-Out (FIFO).
technicalExplanation: A Queue is a FIFO data structure. Elements are inserted at the `Rear` and removed from the `Front`. A simple array-based linear queue suffers from false overflow (space is available at the front, but rear has reached the end). A Circular Queue solves this using modulo arithmetic. Priority Queues order elements by priority rather than insertion order (typically implemented using Heaps). Deques (Double-Ended Queues) allow insertion and deletion at both ends.

definitions.definition: First-In, First-Out. The first element added is the first one removed.
An array implementation where the end connects back to the beginning to reuse empty spaces.

steps.title: Enqueue in Circular Queue
steps.description: Check if full. If not, `rear = (rear + 1) % N`, then `Q[rear] = value`.

steps.title: Dequeue in Circular Queue
steps.description: Check if empty. If not, `value = Q[front]`, then `front = (front + 1) % N`.

formula.explanation: Condition to check if a circular queue is full (assuming one slot is kept empty to distinguish between full and empty states).
formula.whenToUse: Before enqueuing in a circular queue.

formula.explanation: Condition to check if the circular queue is empty.
formula.whenToUse: Before dequeuing in a circular queue.

solvedExamples.solution: 3 Enqueues: rear becomes $(0+3) \% 5 = 3$. 1 Dequeue: front becomes $(0+1) \% 5 = 1$. Result: `front = 1`, `rear = 3`.
solvedExamples.question: In a circular queue of size 5, initially `front = rear = 0`. What are the values of front and rear after 3 Enqueues and 1 Dequeue?

traps: Confusing linear queue full condition (`rear == N-1`) with circular queue full condition (`(rear + 1) % N == front`).
Assuming a queue requires $O(N)$ time for dequeue if implemented as an array (a floating `front` pointer makes it $O(1)$).
takeaways: Queues follow FIFO (First-In, First-Out).
Enqueue happens at the Rear; Dequeue happens at the Front.
Circular queues use modulo arithmetic `(index + 1) % N` to wrap around.
To distinguish between full and empty in a circular array, either keep one slot empty or maintain a `count` variable.
Priority queues are best implemented using Heaps, not linear arrays.

quickRecall.question: What principle does a queue follow?
How do you calculate the next position of `rear` in a circular queue of size $N$?
What data structure is typically used to implement a Priority Queue?

topics.title: Trees and Traversals
topics.whyItMatters: Tree traversal outputs (Pre/In/Post) and reconstructing trees from traversals are staple questions in every CS exam.
understandSimply: A tree represents a hierarchy. Traversals are just different rules for which order to visit the parent node compared to its children.
technicalExplanation: A Binary Tree is a tree where each node has at most two children. The height of a tree is the length of the longest path from the root to a leaf. Traversals visit every node: Preorder (Root, Left, Right), Inorder (Left, Root, Right), Postorder (Left, Right, Root), and Level-order (BFS, using a Queue). A tree can be uniquely reconstructed if Inorder is provided along with either Preorder or Postorder.

definitions.definition: Every node has either 0 or 2 children.
All levels are fully filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.

steps.title: Reconstruct from Inorder and Preorder
steps.description: The first element in Preorder is the Root.

steps.title: Partition the Inorder
steps.description: Find the Root in Inorder. Elements to its left form the Left Subtree; elements to its right form the Right Subtree.

steps.title: Recurse
steps.description: Apply the same logic to the subsets using the next elements in the Preorder sequence.

formula.explanation: Minimum nodes in a binary tree of height h (skewed tree).
formula.whenToUse: When asked for extreme structural bounds.

formula.explanation: Maximum nodes in a binary tree of height h (perfect binary tree).
formula.whenToUse: To find the capacity of a tree.

formula.explanation: In any binary tree, the number of leaf nodes is exactly one more than the number of nodes with two children.

solvedExamples.solution: Root is A. Inorder splits to Left(`D B E`), Right(`F C`). Left subtree Preorder is `B D E` (Root B). B splits Inorder to `D` (left) and `E` (right). Right subtree Preorder is `C F` (Root C). C splits Inorder to `F` (left) and nothing (right). Postorder is Left, Right, Root: `D E B F C A`.
solvedExamples.question: Inorder: `D B E A F C`. Preorder: `A B D E C F`. Find Postorder.

traps: Thinking you can reconstruct a tree uniquely using only Preorder and Postorder (you cannot, Inorder is required).
Confusing height definitions (some textbooks say single node is height 0, others say height 1. GATE usually uses height as number of *edges*).
takeaways: Inorder traversal of a Binary Search Tree (BST) always yields a sorted sequence.
Preorder visits Root first; Postorder visits Root last.
Level-order traversal requires a Queue.
To uniquely reconstruct a binary tree, you MUST have the Inorder traversal.
In a strict binary tree, $L = I_2 + 1$ (Leaves = nodes with 2 children + 1).

quickRecall.question: Which traversal requires a Queue to implement?
Can a tree be uniquely built from Preorder and Postorder traversals?
quickRecall.answer: No, Inorder is required to determine the left/right boundaries.

quickRecall.question: What is the relation between leaf nodes and degree-2 nodes in any binary tree?

topics.title: Binary Search Trees (BST)
topics.whyItMatters: BST properties and the consequences of inserting sorted data are classic complexity questions.
understandSimply: A BST is a sorted tree. Everything smaller goes to the left, everything larger goes to the right. Finding something is like searching a dictionary.
technicalExplanation: A Binary Search Tree dictates that for every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller, and all keys in the right subtree are larger. Search, Insertion, and Deletion average $O(\log N)$ time, but degrade to $O(N)$ worst-case if the tree becomes skewed (e.g., inserting already sorted data). Deleting a node with two children requires replacing it with its Inorder Predecessor (max of left subtree) or Inorder Successor (min of right subtree).

definitions.definition: The node with the smallest key greater than the current node's key (leftmost node in the right subtree).
A tree where every node has at most one child, behaving like a linked list.

steps.title: Delete Node with 2 Children
steps.description: Locate the node to be deleted.

steps.title: Find Replacement
steps.description: Find the Inorder Successor (min value in right subtree) OR Inorder Predecessor (max value in left subtree).

steps.title: Swap and Delete
steps.description: Replace the node's value with the replacement's value, then recursively delete the replacement node (which will have at most 1 child).

solvedExamples.solution: Root is 10. 5 is left of 10. 20 is right of 10. 30 is right of 20. 25 is left of 30. The longest path is 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 25, which has 3 edges. Height = 3.
solvedExamples.question: Insert 10, 5, 20, 30, 25 into an empty BST. What is the height (counting edges)?

solvedExamples.solution: $O(N)$. This occurs when the tree is highly skewed, acting like a linked list.
solvedExamples.question: What is the worst-case time complexity to search in a BST?

traps: Assuming BST operations are always $O(\log N)$ (they are $O(N)$ in the worst case).
When deleting a node with two children, replacing it with an arbitrary child instead of the inorder successor/predecessor.
takeaways: Inorder traversal of a BST outputs elements in sorted (ascending) order.
Worst-case complexity for Search/Insert/Delete is $O(N)$ for skewed trees.
Inserting elements that are already sorted (ascending or descending) creates a worst-case skewed tree.
Deleting a leaf is $O(1)$ after finding it.
Balanced BSTs (like AVL or Red-Black trees) guarantee $O(\log N)$ operations.

quickRecall.question: What traversal of a BST gives a sorted output?
What is the worst-case time complexity for inserting into a standard BST?
How do you replace a deleted node that has two children?
quickRecall.answer: Use its Inorder Predecessor or Inorder Successor.

topics.title: Binary Heaps
topics.whyItMatters: Heaps are the standard implementation for Priority Queues and Heap Sort. Indexing math is frequently tested.
understandSimply: A heap is a complete binary tree where the parent is always "stronger" (larger in max-heap, smaller in min-heap) than its children. It's perfectly balanced and stored in an array.
technicalExplanation: A Binary Heap is a Complete Binary Tree that satisfies the Heap Property. In a Max-Heap, every parent $\ge$ its children. It is stored flat in an array without pointers. Finding the max is $O(1)$. Extracting the max or inserting an element takes $O(\log N)$ time to restore the heap property (Heapify). Building a heap from an unsorted array takes $O(N)$ time.

definitions.definition: The process of adjusting a tree structure to maintain the heap property.
A tree where all levels are completely filled except the last, which is filled left-to-right.

steps.title: Insert into Heap
steps.description: Place the new element at the very end of the array (bottom level, left-most open spot).

steps.title: Bubble Up
steps.description: Compare it with its parent. If it violates the heap property, swap them. Repeat until the property holds.

steps.title: Extract Max
steps.description: Replace the root with the last element in the array. Reduce array size by 1. Bubble the new root down by swapping it with its largest child.

formula.explanation: Index of the left child (assuming 1-based array indexing).
Index of the right child (assuming 1-based array indexing).
Index of the parent node (assuming 1-based array indexing).

solvedExamples.solution: Extract 50. Move last element (35) to root. Array: `[35, 30, 40, 10, 20]`. 35 violates Max-Heap because child 40 > 35. Swap 35 and 40. Array: `[40, 30, 35, 10, 20]`. Heap property is restored.
solvedExamples.question: Given a Max-Heap array (1-indexed): `[50, 30, 40, 10, 20, 35]`. We extract the max. What is the array after restoring the heap?

traps: Confusing 0-based and 1-based indexing formulas. For 0-based: Left = $2i+1$, Right = $2i+2$, Parent = $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$.
Assuming a heap is completely sorted. (Left child can be greater or less than right child).
takeaways: Heaps are Complete Binary Trees, ensuring height is strictly $O(\log N)$.
Heaps are usually implemented using Arrays, not pointers.
Insert and Delete(Extract) take $O(\log N)$ time.
Building a heap from an unsorted array is $O(N)$, not $O(N \log N)$.
Heaps only guarantee the root is the max/min. There is no horizontal order.

quickRecall.question: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an array of size $N$?
In a 1-based array heap, what is the index of the parent of node $i$?
Is a binary heap a strictly sorted data structure?
quickRecall.answer: No, it only maintains a parent-child partial ordering.

topics.title: Graph Representations
topics.whyItMatters: Choosing between matrix and list representation determines the space and time complexity of almost every graph algorithm.
understandSimply: You can map cities (nodes) and roads (edges) either by maintaining a grid showing every possible connection (Matrix), or by keeping a list for each city showing only its actual neighbors (Adjacency List).
technicalExplanation: A Graph $G=(V, E)$ can be Directed or Undirected. An Adjacency Matrix uses a $|V| \times |V|$ 2D array, taking $O(V^2)$ space, allowing $O(1)$ edge lookups. An Adjacency List uses an array of linked lists, taking $O(V + E)$ space, which is far more efficient for sparse graphs. The Handshaking Lemma states that the sum of degrees of all vertices equals $2|E|$ for undirected graphs.

definitions.definition: A 2D array where $M[i][j] = 1$ if there is an edge from $i$ to $j$, else 0.
An array of lists, where the $i$-th list contains all vertices adjacent to vertex $i$.

steps.title: Determine Graph Density
steps.description: Count edges $E$ relative to vertices $V$.

steps.title: Choose Representation
steps.description: If $E$ is close to $V^2$ (Dense), use an Adjacency Matrix. If $E$ is close to $V$ (Sparse), use an Adjacency List.

steps.title: Analyze Operations
steps.description: Matrix is fast for checking if an edge exists $O(1)$. List is fast for iterating over neighbors.

formula.explanation: The Handshaking Lemma for undirected graphs.
formula.whenToUse: To relate the degrees of vertices to the total number of edges.

solvedExamples.solution: Sum of degrees = $2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 16$. By handshaking lemma, $2E = 16$. Therefore, $E = 8$ edges.
solvedExamples.question: An undirected graph has 5 vertices with degrees 2, 3, 3, 4, 4. How many edges does it have?

solvedExamples.solution: $O(\text{degree}(u))$ because you must traverse the linked list of $u$'s neighbors.
solvedExamples.question: Time complexity to find if edge $(u,v)$ exists in an Adjacency List?

traps: Forgetting that in an undirected graph's adjacency list, each edge $(u,v)$ appears twice (once in $u$'s list, once in $v$'s list).
Assuming checking edge existence is $O(1)$ in an Adjacency List.
takeaways: Adjacency Matrix takes $O(V^2)$ space; best for dense graphs.
Adjacency List takes $O(V+E)$ space; best for sparse graphs.
Sum of degrees in an undirected graph is always even ($2E$).
In a directed graph, Sum of In-Degrees = Sum of Out-Degrees = $E$.
A complete graph on $V$ vertices has $V(V-1)/2$ edges.
